anomaly_def.Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + Database Memory Allocation Anomaly
anomaly_def.Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly: Application-level SQL or transaction design obliges the engine to scan, join, or retain far more data and for longer periods than business logic really requires.
Optimizer Statistics Anomaly: The optimizer’s metadata about row counts, data distribution, and correlations is stale or incomplete, leading to systematic cardinality misestimates and poor plan choices.
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly: Aggregate memory consumed by buffer caches, plan caches, per-query work areas, parallel workers, and background heaps grows beyond the host’s safe limit, provoking paging, swapping, or OOM events.

When all three root causes co-exist, the system exhibits extreme and erratic response times, sudden plan regressions, and node-level memory pressure. Queries already oversized by sub-optimal SQL logic are further mis-planned into hash joins, large sorts, or wide index scans because the optimizer under- or over-estimates cardinalities. These memory-hungry operators inflate work-area allocations, evict useful buffer pages, and bloat the plan cache with many ad-hoc variants generated by chatty application patterns. Concurrent long-running transactions keep locks and row versions alive, preventing page reuse and amplifying cache churn, while the OS shows sustained swap, NUMA rebalancing, or even process kills. End-users observe cascading timeouts, increased retry storms, and sporadic service unavailability that are difficult to attribute to a single layer.

Causally, inefficient SQL constructs expand the data footprint and prolong transaction lifetimes; stale or poor statistics mislead the optimizer into choosing memory-intensive physical operations on those inflated datasets; the resulting excessive work-memory grants, spilling, and cache growth breach physical limits, triggering memory pressure and reclaim cycles. Memory stress in turn slows automatic statistics refresh and intensifies plan cache bloat, locking the system into a feedback loop where each anomaly reinforces the others and degrades overall workload stability.

entry.official_definition: Specifies how long transmitted data may remain unacknowledged before the TCP connection is forcibly closed.
entry.trigger_condition: TCP data sent by PostgreSQL remains unacknowledged longer than tcp_user_timeout on systems supporting TCP_USER_TIMEOUT.
entry.workload_impact: The TCP connection is forcibly closed.
entry.default_behavior: Default value is 0, selecting the operating system default.
entry.cause_analysis: This timeout is usually triggered when connection establishment, authentication exchange, or session activity does not progress within the allowed time budget.
entry.solution_guidance: Check connection lifecycle, client responsiveness, authentication latency, idle-session handling, and whether connection pools are holding stale sessions.
